name: Stock Trading System
description: Design a stock exchange/trading platform like NYSE or Robinhood. Covers order matching engine, real-time market data, risk checks, and trade settlement.

learnSteps.title: Order Flow and Risk Validation
learnSteps.description: Trading clients submit orders (buy/sell, limit/market) through the API Gateway, which performs pre-trade risk checks: margin validation, position limits, and circuit breaker thresholds. Validated orders are forwarded to the Order Service, which assigns a sequence number and publishes to the Order Book Queue. Strict ordering per symbol is maintained via Kafka partition keys.

learnSteps.title: Matching Engine (Price-Time Priority)
learnSteps.description: The Matching Engine (Flink) consumes orders from Kafka and maintains an in-memory order book per symbol — sorted buy orders (descending price) and sell orders (ascending price). When a buy price >= sell price, a trade executes. This is the price-time priority algorithm. The engine processes millions of matches per second with exactly-once guarantees via Flink checkpointing.

learnSteps.title: Trade Settlement and Persistence
learnSteps.description: Executed trades are written to PostgreSQL (trade records, position updates, P&L) and TimescaleDB (tick-by-tick market data, OHLCV candles). PostgreSQL uses serializable transactions for settlement correctness. TimescaleDB enables efficient time-range queries for charts and analytics. Both writes happen asynchronously from the matching engine's critical path.

learnSteps.title: Real-Time Market Data Distribution
learnSteps.description: After each trade, the latest price is pushed to the Redis cache with a 1-second TTL. Trading clients poll or subscribe (via WebSocket) for real-time quotes. The Price Cache serves as a read-optimized layer, handling millions of price lookups per second. TimescaleDB feeds the cache with aggregated price updates, ensuring consistency between tick data and displayed quotes.

chaosScenarios.name: Matching Engine JobManager Crash
chaosScenarios.description: The Flink matching engine crashes mid-session and must restore from its last checkpoint, halting all order matching during recovery
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Matching halts for 10-30s while the job restores from the last checkpoint (up to 1s of orders replayed from Kafka). Orders continue to accumulate in the Order Book Queue. Price Cache quotes go stale because no new trades execute. Exactly-once semantics prevent duplicate fills on replay.
mitigationSteps: Gateway circuit breaker pauses new order acceptance (trading halt semantics)
Restore Flink job from last completed checkpoint and replay Kafka from committed offsets
Reconcile engine state against persisted trades in PostgreSQL before resuming
Resume order intake gradually with per-symbol rate limits

chaosScenarios.name: Kafka Broker Loss on Hot Partitions
chaosScenarios.description: A broker hosting leaders for high-volume symbol partitions dies, forcing leader election while producers block on acks=all
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Order submission latency spikes from ~1ms to 1-5s for affected symbols during leader election. ISR shrinks; with min.insync.replicas enforced, no acknowledged orders are lost. Per-symbol ordering is preserved because partition assignment does not change.
mitigationSteps: Automatic leader election promotes in-sync replicas
Order Service retries publishes with idempotent producer enabled
Verify under-replicated partition count returns to zero before declaring recovery
Replace failed broker and trigger partition reassignment off-peak

chaosScenarios.name: Market Open Quote Stampede
chaosScenarios.description: At market open, quote lookups spike 20x while 1-second TTLs on the Price Cache expire simultaneously, stampeding the read path
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Redis CPU saturates on the hottest symbol keys. Cache misses cascade to TimescaleDB aggregation queries. Quote latency p99 degrades from 1ms to 50ms+. Order flow is unaffected because it bypasses the quote path.
mitigationSteps: Pre-warm the Price Cache with opening auction prices before 9:30
Enable request coalescing so one rebuild serves all waiters per symbol
Add jitter to TTL expiry to spread refresh load
Shed quote-polling traffic before order traffic if saturation persists

bottleneckProgression.description: Order Service CPU saturates on validation, sequencing, and risk-check fan-out
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale Order Service instances horizontally; risk checks are stateless per order

bottleneckProgression.description: Kafka cluster approaches its 500 MB/s throughput ceiling as order volume grows
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add brokers, enable producer compression, and split cold symbols to a second cluster

bottleneckProgression.description: Matching engine subtasks pinned to hot symbol partitions saturate; per-symbol matching cannot be parallelized further
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Isolate the hottest symbols onto dedicated high-clock-speed task slots; scale parallelism for the long tail

bottleneckProgression.description: Tick-by-tick ingest into TimescaleDB falls behind during volatility spikes
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Batch tick inserts, enable compression on older chunks, and move OHLCV rollups to continuous aggregates

expectedIssues.title: Hot Symbol Partition Skew
expectedIssues.description: A single viral symbol (meme-stock event) concentrates order flow onto one Kafka partition and one matching engine subtask, capping throughput for that symbol regardless of cluster size
expectedIssues.mitigation: Dedicated task slots for hot symbols, per-symbol rate limiting at the gateway, and queue-depth alerts keyed by partition

expectedIssues.title: Stale Position Data in Pre-Trade Risk Checks
expectedIssues.description: Gateway risk checks read cached positions; during settlement write lag a trader can submit orders against margin already consumed, passing checks that should fail
expectedIssues.mitigation: Bound the staleness window with synchronous position reservations for large orders; reconcile and auto-liquidate breaches post-trade

expectedIssues.title: Settlement Write Lag Under Peak Load
expectedIssues.description: Async trade persistence to PostgreSQL falls behind the matching engine during peak volume; serializable transaction retries compound the backlog and delay P&L visibility
expectedIssues.mitigation: Batch trade inserts per symbol, monitor settlement lag as a first-class SLO, and alert before the lag exceeds the checkpoint retention window

expectedIssues.title: Stale Quotes Displayed During Engine Recovery
expectedIssues.description: While the matching engine restores from checkpoint, the Price Cache continues serving last-known prices with no staleness indicator, misleading traders
expectedIssues.mitigation: Publish a market-state flag (open/halted/recovering) alongside quotes; clients must render stale-price warnings when the flag is not 'open'

components.label: Matching Engine (Flink)
components.costDriver: 64-slot Flink cluster on memory-optimized instances with checkpoint storage

components.label: Trade DB (PostgreSQL)
components.costDriver: Multi-AZ primary + 3 replicas, 5TB provisioned IOPS storage

components.label: API Gateway (Risk Check)
components.costDriver: Self-hosted gateway fleet sized for 100k RPS rate limiting + JWT auth

metrics.name: order_ack_latency
metrics.description: Time from order receipt to sequenced acknowledgement

metrics.name: match_throughput
metrics.description: Trades executed per second by the matching engine

metrics.description: Age of the freshest price per symbol in the Price Cache

metrics.description: Delay between trade execution and PostgreSQL persistence

steps: Halt new order intake at the API Gateway (declare trading pause)
Confirm last completed Flink checkpoint and committed Kafka offsets
Restore the job and replay; verify no duplicate fills via trade sequence numbers
Reconcile engine order book state against PostgreSQL trade records
Resume intake gradually per symbol and notify compliance of the halt window

runbooks.incident: Kafka consumer lag spike on hot symbol
steps: Identify the lagging partition and its symbol
Check broker health and ISR status before assuming engine slowness
Apply per-symbol rate limiting at the gateway if a single symbol dominates
Scale matching engine parallelism for unaffected partitions
Verify trades are still executing (rule out engine halt first)
Check the TimescaleDB-to-cache update pipeline for backlog
Set the market-state flag to 'degraded' so clients show staleness warnings
Rebuild affected symbol keys from the latest TimescaleDB aggregates

decisions.title: Kafka Partition-per-Symbol for Order Sequencing
decisions.context: Order matching requires strict price-time priority; orders for the same symbol must be processed in arrival order
decisions.decision: Partition the Order Book Queue by symbol key so each symbol's orders flow through exactly one partition and one matching subtask
consequences: Strict per-symbol ordering with no distributed locking
Throughput for any single symbol is capped by one partition/subtask (hot symbol skew)

decisions.title: In-Memory Order Book with Exactly-Once Checkpointing
decisions.context: Matching must run at millions of operations per second; disk-backed order books cannot meet latency targets
decisions.decision: Keep order books entirely in Flink managed state, with 1s checkpoints providing exactly-once recovery from Kafka offsets
consequences: Crash recovery replays at most ~1s of orders, bounded and deterministic
Checkpoint duration becomes a critical health signal — slow checkpoints precede outages

decisions.title: Asynchronous Settlement off the Matching Critical Path
decisions.context: Serializable PostgreSQL writes take milliseconds; placing them inline would cap matching throughput at DB speed
decisions.decision: Persist executed trades to PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB asynchronously after the match is sequenced
consequences: Matching throughput is independent of DB write latency
A settlement lag window exists where positions/P&L trail executions
Risk checks reading positions must tolerate bounded staleness

tradeoffs.benefit: Negligible runtime overhead on the matching hot path
tradeoffs.cost: Up to 1s of orders must be replayed (not lost) on engine failure, extending recovery time

tradeoffs.choice: Redis price cache with 1s TTL serving all quote reads
tradeoffs.benefit: Millions of price lookups per second never touch the time-series store
tradeoffs.cost: Quotes can lag true market state by up to 1s, and go silently stale if the engine halts

tradeoffs.benefit: Deterministic price-time priority without locks or conflict resolution
tradeoffs.cost: A single viral symbol cannot exceed one subtask's throughput no matter how large the cluster

alternatives.name: Monolithic Single-Process Matching Engine (LMAX-style)
alternatives.description: Run the entire order book in one process using a ring-buffer event loop, with replicated state machines for HA
alternatives.prosVsCons: Microsecond-class latency and total determinism, but failover, multi-symbol scaling, and operational tooling must all be built from scratch
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Flink provides checkpointing, replay, and horizontal scaling out of the box; this platform targets ms-class retail latency, not HFT microseconds

alternatives.name: Synchronous Per-Trade Database Writes
alternatives.description: Commit each executed trade to PostgreSQL inside the matching transaction before acknowledging
alternatives.prosVsCons: Zero settlement lag and simpler reconciliation, but matching throughput collapses to DB commit rate (~10k/s)
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Would cap the engine two orders of magnitude below target; bounded settlement lag is acceptable and monitored

alternatives.name: Distributed Order Book with Optimistic Concurrency
alternatives.description: Shard the order book across nodes and resolve conflicting matches via compare-and-swap
alternatives.prosVsCons: Removes the per-symbol throughput cap, but conflict retries break price-time fairness guarantees under contention
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Fairness is a regulatory requirement; nondeterministic match ordering under load is disqualifying
